english.html: Besides that it is not probable, for the proximity of blood, that the uncle should not know his own nephew <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, or that he should be so brutal and unnatural as to wish to annihilate and destroy his own blood. It is certain also that no person (unless he be more felonious than the savage beasts) ever held his own flesh in hatred, but maintains, nourishes and preserves it, to the utmost of his power <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Whence Saint Paul called him worse than an infidel who has no care of his own <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 38.8.9 (Unde cognati, l. Octavi, cited as l. octaui); Code, title De in integrum restitutione (one of the restitution titles of Code book 2; the law cited as l. de tutela not identified)
notes.original: l. octaui, D. vnde cog. l. de tutela. C de in integ. reſt.
notes.gloss: Cited for the presumption that near kin know one another.
Nemo enim umquam carnem suam odio habuit, sed nutrit et fovet eam — for no man ever yet hated his own flesh, but nourisheth and cherisheth it.

notes.original: La i. de Ti moth. c. v.
notes.gloss: Si quis autem suorum … curam non habet, fidem negavit et est infideli deterior — if any have not care of his own, he hath denied the faith and is worse than an infidel.

english.html: Which the said Barrau, the uncle, well showed at the exhibition [exhibition: the presenting of the prisoner to him] that was made to him of the prisoner his nephew, as well before the said Judge of Rieux as afterwards in the Court: for, seeing him in the hands of Justice, the heavy irons on his legs, and in danger of his life, he began incontinently to weep and to groan bitterly.

Although sometimes men shed tears from a great and too excessive joy which suddenly presents itself, as did Ptolemy Philadelphus when there were offered to him the laws of the Jews written in letters of gold a2; nevertheless it most often happens that man weeps only from melancholy, vexation and sadness, and then there is great reason for it: for the spirit, which is extremely afflicted with grief and anguish, is carried up as far as the membrane of the brain, where it presses the humour that it finds there, so that it constrains it to go out; and that is why the Latins call the humour that flows down from the eyes LACRIMA, that is to say tear: a word drawn from laceration, which is as much as to say to break, to rend and to consume; for from the breaking and sadness of the spirit the tears are moved and provoked. Alexander of Aphrodisias

notes.citation: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities XII, chapter 2 (12.2.10, §§ 89–90 in the modern division: Ptolemy Philadelphus, shown the Law written in letters of gold, weeps from excess of joy; cf. the Letter of Aristeas §§ 176–178)
notes.original: Ioſephe au liure xij. des Antiquitez Iudaiques c. ij.
notes.gloss: The transcription flags the middle letters of Iudaiques as illegible and supplied from the citation.

du ſang, que l'oncle ne congnoiſſe ſon propre ne pueu
{a}, ou qu'il ſoit ſi brutal & deſnaturé de vouloir anean-
tir & deſtruire ſon propre ſang. Il eſt certain auſsi que
perſonne (ſi elle n'eſt plus felonne que les beſtes ſau-
uages) n'eut oncques en haine ſa chair: mais l'entre-
tient, nourriſt & conſeque, de ſon pouuoir {b}. Dont
ſainct Paul appeloit celuy pire que infidelle, qui n'a
ſoin des ſiens {ſ}.
Ce que ledit Barreau oncle, monſtra
bien à l'exhibition qui luy fut faite du
priſonnier ſon nepueu, tant deuant ledit
Iuge de Rieux, qu'apres en la cour: car le
voyant entre les mains de Iuſtice, les
gros fers aux iambes, & en danger de ſa
vie, ſe mit incontinẽt à pleurer, & gemir
amerement.
Encor que quelquesfois les hommes larmoyent
par vne grande, & trop exceſsiue ioye, qui ſoudain ſe
preſente, comme fit Ptolomee Philadelphe, quand on
luy offrit les loix des Iuifs eſcrites en lettres d'or {a2}:
toutesfois le plus ſouuent aduient, que l'homme ne
pleure que de malancholie, faſcherie, & triſteſſe, & lors
y a grande raiſon: car l'eſprit qui eſt extremement affli
ge d'ẽnuy & engoiſſe, eſt apporté iuſqu'à la pellicule du
cerueau, où il preſſe l'humeur qu'il y trouue: tellemẽt
qu'il la contrainct ſortir dehors: & voila pourquoy les
Latins appellent l'humeur, qui decoule des yeux, LA-
